implementation_notes: Iterator adaptors such as map, filter and filter_map take an Iterator and return another Iterator, so chaining them builds a pipeline; the chain is lazy and only a terminal operation (collect, fold, for_each, sum) drives it (doc.rust-lang.org std::iter). The method chain replaces the classic stage list and the concrete nested adaptor type is the composed pipeline. Fallible stages fit the same shape with Result and and_then/try_collect instead of panics; use the async variant when stages await I/O.
pitfalls: Adaptors are lazy and do nothing until a terminal operation runs, so a forgotten terminal is a silent no-op.
The chain's type is the nested adaptor type: storing or returning a pipeline needs impl Iterator or boxing.
filter followed by map is not fused automatically and iterates twice per element; filter_map exists to fuse fallible transforms.

variants.name: Async stage functions over futures
variants.idiom_name: async fn stages sequenced with .await (or Stream::then)
variants.implementation_notes: When stages perform I/O, each stage becomes an async fn returning a Future, and the pipeline is either one async fn sequencing the awaits or a Stream (futures crate) combined with then/filter_map; futures are inert values that progress only while polled by an executor (doc.rust-lang.org Future). Errors compose through ? and a shared error type rather than through exceptions. Choose this variant when stages cross an I/O boundary; the iterator chain stays the right tool for CPU-bound pure transformations.
pitfalls: Futures do nothing until awaited or spawned, so dropping one cancels the pipeline silently and mid-flight work is lost.
A non-Send value held across an await makes the whole future non-Send and breaks multi-threaded executors.
Stage errors must unify into one type; without an enum or Box<dyn Error> the pipeline stops composing.
